cards.title: Build footer policy and support menus before linking them in the theme
cards.summary: Create Shopify policies and an About page first, then assemble two or three footer link menus and attach them as footer link-list blocks.
cards.use_when: Setting up the store footer so policy, contact and support pages are reachable from every page of the storefront.
steps: Generate every required policy in the Shopify admin under Settings > Policies (terms of service, refund, privacy, shipping). Insert the template for each, review and edit the text so it matches your store, then click Publish — unpublished policies have no URL to link to.

Create the pages you want to link: go to Online Store > Pages and add at least an About Us page (and a contact/support page if the theme's default contact page isn't enough). Save without styling; edit the copy later.

Go to Online Store > Navigation > Menus and create separate menus rather than one long list: for example 'Helpful Links' containing all policies, and 'Quick Links' containing About Us, Contact and support pages. This mirrors how larger retailers split footer navigation into services / help / about columns.

Return to the theme editor, open the footer section, and point each Links block at one of the menus you created. Use the plus between footer blocks to add additional link-list blocks, then rename each block heading (e.g. 'Support') so customers can scan them.
Optionally hide the newsletter block in the footer since popups already capture signups; keep it if the footer is your only email capture point.
caveats: Menu contents are shared across all pages, so any change to a footer menu updates sitewide — double-check links after editing.
The available footer blocks and their naming differ by theme; check the block types your theme actually exposes.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Choose theme sections by first checking the available section library
cards.summary: Inspect the theme's full section library and confirm niche-critical sections exist before committing to a theme.
cards.use_when: Selecting or trialling a Shopify theme, or planning which homepage/PDP/collection sections your store will need.
steps: In the theme editor, hover between two existing sections, click the plus icon and browse the complete list of available sections, grouped by type (banners, collections, forms, info, product lists, etc.).
Note that the default homepage sections a theme ships with are only a subset — you can remove them and add any other available section to any page.

Map your niche requirements against that list before buying the theme. Example: a cosmetics brand needing a before/after gallery must verify the theme offers such a section, since it can't be added later if it doesn't exist.

Confirm which section types are universal vs theme-specific: banners, collection list and featured collection are near-universal, while logo list, multicolumn, testimonials and subcollection blocks vary by theme.
If the exact section is missing, look for generic substitutes — a multicolumn or column block that supports an image, text and link can stand in for a logo list.
caveats: Reconciling this check against the theme store preview is faster than rebuilding later; section availability is a hard constraint, not a styling preference.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Assemble the homepage in a deliberate section order
cards.summary: Build the homepage one section at a time in a sequence that moves from brand message to proof to bestsellers to story, removing theme defaults you don't need.
cards.use_when: Designing or rebuilding the store homepage structure after the header and footer are set.
steps: Start with a slideshow or background video as the first banner. Use it to state what you sell, announce a new collection or drop, and link the image or button directly to that collection — this is the source's recommended way to open a homepage.

Keep the hero simple: one image or video, or at most two to three slides. Use a landscape image for desktop, and upload a separate mobile image if the theme allows it rather than accepting a bad crop.
Follow the hero with a USP or logo-list section: each logo block carries one unique selling proposition (image, title, link). The same section type can show certifications or press logos.
Add a featured-collection section for your bestsellers. The source's stated position is that bestsellers are bestsellers for a reason, so showing them on the homepage is always recommended.
Continue with collection list, image-with-text linking to the About page, and a testimonial section populated with the strongest real reviews and optional customer photos.
Add remaining sections only as needed (blog, rich text) and delete the theme's default filler — a shorter, intentional homepage is preferred over keeping everything the theme shipped.
caveats: The recommended section sequence is the presenter's design opinion, not a tested universal rule; adapt to your catalogue and traffic source.
Testimonial sections can also come from an app via app blocks; the theme's built-in section just avoids the dependency.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Set hero slideshow height and focal point to prevent bad crops
cards.summary: Control slideshow height, per-device images and image focal points so the hero looks intentional on desktop and mobile.
cards.use_when: Configuring a homepage hero slideshow or banner section where images crop awkwardly across devices.
steps: Click the slideshow section (not the individual slide) to reach its general settings, then choose a height mode: full screen, adapt to first image, or fixed height.
Prefer 'adapt to first image' if you uploaded images at the correct dimensions — this shows the full image without cropping.

If you need a consistent band instead, use fixed height. The source's working example used around 600px on both desktop and mobile; treat that number as a starting point, not a benchmark, and check both viewports.
For images that still crop badly, open the image in the editor and set the focal point on the part that must survive cropping (e.g. a model's face). The theme then crops around that point.
Set a separate mobile image where the theme supports it, and give each slide a full-slide link as an alternative to a button if you don't want a visible CTA.
Check the mobile preview after each change; text-below-image on mobile is discouraged when a dedicated mobile image is available.
caveats: Fixed-height values and the availability of mobile-specific images, focal points and text-below settings vary by theme; verify in your theme's editor.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use duplicate and copy-paste to build section sets quickly and consistently
cards.summary: Duplicate blocks to inherit identical dimensions, and copy entire sections between pages so shared layouts stay consistent.
cards.use_when: Building repetitive section structures such as logo lists, USP rows or cross-page content bands in the theme editor.
steps: Set the first block up completely — including image width — then use Duplicate to create siblings. Duplicated blocks inherit the same dimensions, so you only swap the image/text instead of resizing each one; the source explicitly regrets resizing every logo individually.
Reorder blocks or sections by hovering and dragging them to the new position, including dragging a section to a different point in the page.
To move a section to another page, select it and use Copy, then navigate to the target page and use Paste (or Paste after) — copied sections can be pasted on any Shopify page.
Blocks can only be pasted into a section type that supports that block type, so keep whole reusable layouts at section level.
Edit block text either through the settings panel or by turning on direct editing and double-clicking the text on the canvas.
caveats: Section copy/paste between pages is a newer Shopify editor capability; interface details may change, so verify it exists in your editor version.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Create a bestsellers collection with tags and feature it
cards.summary: Tag chosen products, build an automated tag-based bestsellers collection, and render it via a featured-collection section.
cards.use_when: Adding a bestsellers or curated homepage product row when the store has no existing bestsellers collection.
steps: Decide which products to feature, then tag them (e.g. tag equal to 'bestsellers') using Select all > Bulk edit > add tag in the products list.
Go to Products > Collections and create a collection named 'bestsellers' with an automated condition of tag equals bestsellers, then save.

In the theme editor, add a Featured Collection section and select the bestsellers collection. Some themes let you select individual products instead of a collection; this workflow assumes collection-only selection.
Where the theme supports it, change the section's colour scheme to differentiate the band from adjacent sections and check badge styling in each scheme.
Later, maintain the tag as your real bestsellers change — the section updates automatically because the collection is condition-based.
caveats: The source recommends showing bestsellers on the homepage; if you have little or no sales data, define 'bestseller' by your own judgement or omit the label rather than implying sales volume you don't have.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Build automated collections with AND-style tag conditions
cards.summary: Create one collection from multiple tag conditions so products tagged with any of several values all appear in a single category.
cards.use_when: Building a parent category (e.g. all activewear) that should gather several product types tagged separately.
steps: In Products > Collections, create a new collection and choose automated conditions rather than manual selection.

Decide whether products must match ALL conditions or ANY condition. To pool leggings, bras and overalls into one activewear collection, set 'any condition' with separate rules: tag equals leggings, tag equals bra, tag equals overall.
Save and verify the product count matches expectations; the collection updates automatically as tags change.
Keep tag values consistent in the product data or products will silently fall out of the collection.
caveats: Using 'any condition' is the opposite of what you'd want for narrowing rules; mixing ALL and ANY logic carelessly produces either over-broad or empty collections.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Configure collection filters using Shopify Search & Discovery
cards.summary: Add product-type, size, colour and other filters via the Search & Discovery app, then make sure the underlying product data is populated.
cards.use_when: Setting up collection page filtering so shoppers can narrow a large catalogue by type, size, colour or price.
steps: In Shopify admin, open the Search & Discovery app > Filters and add the filters you want (standard fields such as product type and size, plus custom ones like fabric or colour).

Fill in the underlying product data for filters to return results. A filter with only one value in the admin usually means you haven't entered product type (or the relevant field) on the other products — bulk-edit products to populate it.
Write values consistently: 'legging' and 'leggings' create two separate filter options, so standardise the wording across products.
Order filters in the app (e.g. product type before fabric, size where it fits logically) and save; order is controlled from the app, not the theme.
In the theme editor's collection template, review theme-level filter settings — some themes render certain filters as buttons (e.g. sizes) and may support colour swatches natively.
caveats: Filter display options vary by theme; the app determines which filters exist and their order, the theme determines how they render.
Price is available as a filter but the source's example set also leaned on product data quality, which is the usual failure point.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Turn on colour swatches with defined colours or variant images
cards.summary: Expose variant colours on collection product cards using either named colour swatches with hex values or automatically pulled variant images.
cards.use_when: Collection-page merchandising when products come in multiple colours but the cards show no colour indication.
steps: In the theme editor, open the product card/swatch settings inside the collection template (or theme settings > swatches) and enable swatches.

For hex-based swatches: select the colour-list option, then define each variant colour name and its hex code (look the code up by searching e.g. 'red hex'). The swatch appears once the name matches the variant value.
For image swatches: select the variant-image option so the theme pulls the actual variant image, which the source preferred for its store.

For custom swatch graphics (e.g. patterns rather than flat colours), upload an image named exactly after the variant value with the correct extension (e.g. red.png) and the theme will use it in place of the colour.
Save and open the live/collection preview to confirm swatches appear under the product cards.
caveats: Swatch configuration differs across themes, though all common themes support swatches; if they don't show, a setting is usually unset rather than unsupported.
Variant naming must match swatch names exactly for the association to work.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Work on the default collection template first, then branch to custom templates
cards.summary: Set universal collection settings once in the default template, then create named templates for collections that need extra sections.
cards.use_when: Deciding between editing the shared default collection layout and creating per-collection layouts.
steps: Open the theme editor's Collections section; the Default collection template applies to every collection assigned to it (the source observed six collections sharing one template).

Configure the shared settings there: show/hide collection title and image, heading image height, overlay style, show/hide description, products per page, products per row, and whether to show vendor and product count.
Add the description and collection image if you care about SEO, since these feed the collection page content.
Set the default sort (bestselling, alphabetical, price low to high) in the collection section settings.
Where a collection needs different content or extra sections, click Create template in the Collections area, name it after the collection (e.g. 'activewear'), and build its sections.
Assign the template per collection in the admin; if the theme isn't published yet, template assignment may not be visible, so plan to assign after publishing.
caveats: Changes to the default template affect every collection assigned to it — a common source of unintended sitewide edits.
Template assignment options depend on whether the theme is published.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Add a visual subcollection row with a multicolumn section
cards.summary: Simulate subcollection navigation by duplicating a multicolumn block per subcollection, each with image and link, at the top of a custom collection template.
cards.use_when: Large catalogues where a parent collection needs to route shoppers into leggings/bras/overalls-style subsections.
steps: Create a dedicated collection template for the parent collection and preview that collection against it.
Add a multicolumn section above the product grid, delete all but one block, then fully configure the first: image, title (e.g. Leggings) and a link to that subcollection.
Set the media width to a consistent, small size on the first block, then Duplicate it for each remaining subcollection and swap the image, title and link — duplicating preserves the dimensions.
Hide the parent collection's own title and product count in the template settings so the subcollection row reads as the page's primary navigation.
Optionally add a rich-text section above the row with an instruction such as 'select by product type' and its own heading removed, to avoid repeating the collection title.
Use product images with transparent backgrounds where possible for a cleaner subcollection row, as seen on reference stores using the same theme.
caveats: Native subcollection blocks exist in some themes but not all; the multicolumn approach is the portable fallback.
This template must then be assigned to the specific collection in the admin once the theme is published.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use collection metafields to vary content inside a shared collection template
cards.summary: Define collection metafields for image, title, text and link, then connect section fields to dynamic sources so one layout shows different promotional content per collection.
cards.use_when: Running one collection layout with a promotion or lookbook band whose content must differ per collection.
steps: Decide which section elements need to vary (image, heading, body text, button link). Anything left static will show the same on every collection using that template.

In Settings > Metafields and metaobjects > Collections, add definitions: an image-type field (e.g. 'promotion section image'), a single-line text field for the heading, a rich-text field for the body, and a URL-type field for the button link.

In the theme editor, click the section element and use 'connect dynamic source' to bind it to the metafield — the section field only accepts metafield types it supports (an image field won't accept a text metafield, and a link field may require the URL type).
Fill the metafields per collection in the admin (individually or via bulk edit with the metafield columns exposed), then save.
Preview two different collections sharing the template to confirm the layout is identical but the content changes; empty metafields render as nothing.
caveats: If a metafield doesn't appear as a selectable dynamic source, the defined type is wrong for that field — redefine it as URL vs link, single-line vs rich text, etc.
Use templates, not metafields, when the whole layout must differ; metafields are for dynamic content within a shared layout.
Metafield linking is easier once the theme is published and the collection admin fields are visible.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Research competitor PDPs and reviews before designing your product page
cards.summary: Derive the sections and proof points for your product page from big competitors' structures and from customer questions and objections in reviews.
cards.use_when: Planning a product page layout or rewriting PDP content, especially before building a new template.
steps: List the sections and information blocks you plan to include before touching the theme editor.
Audit competitor stores in your niche — prioritise large brands, on the reasoning that they have tested their PDP structures extensively and their choices indicate what customers care about.
Read reviews on competitor sites and on Amazon to extract the specific questions, hesitations and objections customers raise before buying.

Translate each objection into a PDP element. The source's example: a client selling a premium pasta knew taste was the core objection, so the page needed reviews and people visibly tasting and endorsing the product.
Handle the price objection the same way: the pasta was roughly three times the price of supermarket pasta, so the page had to prove health and quality benefits to justify it.
caveats: Competitor structure is a research input, not a template to copy wholesale; and the pasta example is an illustration of the method, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx

cards.title: Use Sidekick to make editor changes — with eyes open about scope
cards.summary: Ask Shopify's Sidekick to modify a section's settings from inside the theme editor, but verify that the change hasn't leaked into other sections.
cards.use_when: Making quick visual tweaks to a homepage or PDP section when you're not yet comfortable with theme settings.
steps: Open the theme editor, select the section you want to change, and use the 'ask for changes' option to describe the change (e.g. make the button text red and 25% larger, or restyle a grid as vintage).
Review the result on the canvas; if you don't like it, keep asking for further adjustments or use the full chat to see and redo prior changes.

After any Sidekick change, check other sections of the store that share the same setting — for example, a heading colour change may propagate to headings everywhere depending on how the theme defines them.
For anything structural or precise, edit the theme settings yourself; the source's view is that manual theme control is still preferable, with Sidekick as a beginner aid.
caveats: Sidekick updates theme settings, not code, so its reach is limited by how the theme shares settings across sections.
This feature evolves quickly — verify its current behaviour and options in your editor.
cards.source_name: Shopify for Beginners_ Everything From Setup to Your First Sale.docx
